newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Clashes spread between Sierra Leone army, hunters.
newsitem.headline: Clashes spread between Sierra Leone army, hunters.

text.p: At least 14 people died in overnight fighting in northern Sierra Leone between the army and a hunters' militia, military authorities said on Monday.
"So far the army has found 14 bodies of soldiers and Kapras (hunters) at Camp Charlie, but most of the bodies are Kapras," said one military source.
Army Chief of Staff Lieutenant-Colonel Max Kanga told Reuters that hundreds of hunters on Sunday evening attacked the main military base in the north at Camp Charlie, 90 miles (145 km) from Freetown.
"There was a serious shoot-out which lasted for six hours," he said in the capital.
The death toll from a weekend clash between the army and a seperate group of hunters in the eastern town of Kenema had risen to 20 on Monday, military sources said by telephone from the town.
There is traditional rivalry between the hunters and regular troops who fought together against rebels of the Revolutionary United Front, but no immediate cause is known for the most recent clashes.
At the weekend thousands of civilians fled Kenema as hunters, known in the south and east as Kamajors, fought soldiers in the streets with rocket propelled grenades and heavy machine guns.

Relief agencies in Freetown said on Monday that most of their workers had been evacuated from Kenema by helicopter. Three staff from the International Committee of the Red Cross stayed behind to treat the wounded.
Kanga said a truce had been arranged with the hunters in Kenema late on Sunday night and that the streets of the diamond-mining town were calm.
To establish the cause of the clashes between the former allies, President Ahmed Tejan Kabbah has set up a six-man commission of inquiry, national radio announced on Sunday.
Kanga said the army was being attacked because the government had not put adequate structures in place to keep the militias under control and punish them if they broke the law.
"The government must do so if they are to permanently resolve the clashes," he said.
A peace deal between Tejan Kabbah and rebel leader Foday Sankoh was signed in November to try and end the civil war which erupted in 1991.
But implementation of the deal has dragged, threatening to unravel the peace process.
